system_prompt:
You are distilling one chapter of a guitar method book into a short summary.

The user will give you a chapter file with topic-organized verbatim quotes
plus the human-rationale notes for each. Write a one-paragraph summary (4-7
sentences) that captures:

  - what this chapter teaches (the techniques, concepts, rules, examples)
  - the master's characteristic moves visible in this chapter (if any)
  - the load-bearing terminology this chapter introduces

Reference the topic labels from the chapter file when useful. Do not invent
information not present in the chapter. If the chapter is biographical or
introductory rather than instructional, say so explicitly.

Output just the paragraph — no preamble, no JSON, no markdown formatting.

Chapter 18: Professional Fingerstyle Jazz Guitar, Part 7: Fun Jazz

<<<CHAPTER FILE
# Chapter 18 — Professional Fingerstyle Jazz Guitar, Part 7: Fun Jazz

_Pages 168-184._

> **Verbatim-quote constraint.** The quotes below are exact substrings of the raw transcript produced by `pdftotext`. The transcript may contain extraction artifacts where the book's typeface confuses the tool — e.g. `7irst` or `<irst` for `first`, `speci7ic` for `specific`. **Do NOT manually fix these in this file**: the quote-fidelity validator compares against the raw transcript, so a 'fixed' quote will fail verification and break Stage 2 idempotency. If a future pipeline iteration adds artifact-normalization, it must normalize the transcript and these files together.

## Chromatic modulation by half step

> The key changes from C to D moving chromatically by half step. Don’t let the chord quality get in
> the way of your analysis. It can be simple or sophisticated.

**Significance (p. 168).** Teaches chromatic half-step modulation, emphasizing that chord quality and root position are flexible.

## Approaching chords by half step

> Approaching a chord from a half step above or belowis another accepted way of moving the harmony.
> The A13 in measure two — the V7 of the new key of D — is approached by Bb13 in the first measure. The
> inner descending line in measure two is interesting enough to stay where itis for four beats before moving

**Significance (p. 168).** Names half-step chord approach as a standard harmonic movement technique, with the V7 of the new key approached from a half step above.

## Within-the-scale cycle (Mozart fakeroo)

> A major scale can within itself provide cyclical movement, although not with
> exact perfect fifth intervals throughout. This within-the-scale cycle is used here
> through the Dm7, after which a’ VI (A’6) of the C scale is inserted. This deceptive
> cadence opens up several possibilities, but since we want to move on to E>, we'll
> stay with the A’6 as the way to go.

**Significance (p. 168).** Describes how the major scale provides an approximate cycle of fifths internally and demonstrates the deceptive cadence as a modulation pivot.

## Trust the ear

> Ultimately, whatever sounds good to the ear will probably work. Just go there. Of course, if all
> your playing buddies grimace, you do have to remember that there are community standards of
> decency.

**Significance (p. 168).** States that ear-based judgment ultimately governs harmonic choices, balanced by ensemble taste.

## Fun Jazz philosophy

> Since being taught to death is a horrible way to die, I've decided to make Part 7 a group of tunes
> without analysis, explanation or instruction. Just a personal word or two. Do | hear cheering?
>
> | call these pieces Fun Jazz, as they were fun for me to create. | didn’t sit down and compose
> them. They are improvisations based on standard chord changes which you may recognize.

**Significance (p. 169).** Frames Part 7 as unanalyzed improvisations over standard changes, shifting from instruction to creative example.

## Imply more with less

> In all of the tunes here | like to imply more with less. Chords, for instance, are most often only
> two or three notes, and the melody is all-important.

**Significance (p. 169).** States the core fingerstyle principle of implying harmony with minimal chord voicings (two or three notes) while prioritizing melody.

## Good evening friends / three voices

> In the days of Vaudeville, musicians used to play a purposely silly ending called "good evening friends." I decided to make the four-note theme into a blues.
> There are three independent voices at once in this piece, if you count a whole note as a voice. It is. Play the piece with an underlying triplet feel.

**Significance (p. 174).** Describes treating three independent voices simultaneously and applying a triplet feel to the piece.

## Stride to bebop (Fats Waller)

> This Fats Waller imitation starts with a solid stride style. After a while I sneak bebop into it. Ragtime bebop? Why not?

**Significance (p. 175).** Demonstrates blending stride piano style with bebop on guitar, crossing genre boundaries.

## Ballad elbow room

> I love ballads. They allow a player to have as much elbow room to do whatever he wants, such as playing in double time feel.

**Significance (p. 178).** Names ballads as the form giving maximum freedom, including double-time feel shifts.

## Sparse blues / Joe Pass device

> This blues is sparse in bass notes yet feels as though nothing is missing. One way this is accom-
> plished is by using an almost continual eighth note flow. Joe Pass often used this device.

**Significance (p. 180).** Credits Joe Pass for the continual eighth-note flow technique that compensates for sparse bass notes in blues.

## Fleshing out single-line improvisation

> This improvisation was included in an earlier book of mine, Jazz in Position (Mel Bay
> Publications, Inc.). That was a book for pick guitar, and the melodic line was just one note with
> no accompaniment. Here | fleshed it out and turned it into a self-accompanied fingerstyle
> arrangement. You can do this with virtually any existing tune you have been playing as a single
> line only. The chord structure is similar to Lullaby of Birdland.

**Significance (p. 181).** Teaches the technique of converting any single-line melody into a self-accompanied fingerstyle arrangement.

## 3 on 4 polyrhythm with tritones

> 3 on 4 takes its name from having many three-beat phrases in the context of 4/4 measures. The melodic line is primarily accompanied by tri-tones. This is the type of sparse playing that could easily fit in a trio or quartet setting.

**Significance (p. 182).** Names the three-over-four polyrhythmic device accompanied by tritones as sparse playing suitable for ensemble contexts.

## Walkdown device

> A walkdown is a descending bass line with a common tone on top of a chord stack. This is the
>
> device that keeps popping up in this tune along with its hook-like rhythm.

**Significance (p. 182).** Defines the walkdown as a descending bass line under a common-tone chord stack, a recurring compositional device.
